root.title: Geometric Deep Learning
root.gist: A single blueprint of symmetry, scale separation, and geometric stability unifies most deep learning architectures across grids, graphs, groups, geodesics, and gauges.
root.question: Geometric Deep Learning — why do so many different neural network architectures share the same underlying structure? (a unifying blueprint)

children.title: Title and contents
children.gist: The paper's title, authors, and table of contents.

children.title: Preface
children.gist: Following Felix Klein's Erlangen Programme, which unified geometries through symmetry groups, the authors propose Geometric Deep Learning to unify neural network architectures through the same symmetry principles.
children.question: Geometric Deep Learning — how can symmetry unify the zoo of deep learning architectures? (a historical analogy)

children.title: Notation
children.gist: A reference table of the mathematical symbols used throughout the text.

children.title: 1 Introduction
children.gist: Deep learning succeeds because high-dimensional tasks of interest are not generic but carry geometric regularities, and exposing these through a shared framework lets researchers derive existing and future architectures from first principles of symmetry.
children.question: Introduction — what principle explains why deep learning works despite the curse of dimensionality? (a unifying framework)

children.title: 2 Learning in High Dimensions
children.gist: Generic high-dimensional learning is cursed by exponential sample complexity, so effective learning requires encoding the right geometric inductive bias into the function class.
children.question: Learning in high dimensions — why can't we learn arbitrary high-dimensional functions from data? (the curse of dimensionality)

children.title: Supervised learning setup
children.gist: Supervised learning estimates an unknown function from samples by choosing, within a parametrised function class, the candidate that minimises expected loss on new data drawn from the same distribution.

children.title: 2.1 Inductive Bias via Function Regularity
children.gist: Even though neural networks can approximate almost any function, good generalisation requires an inductive bias—a complexity measure favoring regular functions—enforced explicitly through regularisation or implicitly by the optimisation procedure.

children.title: 2.2 The Curse of Dimensionality
children.gist: Classical regularity notions like Lipschitz or Sobolev smoothness require exponentially many samples as dimension grows, and even sparsity-based neural network priors fail for real functions with long-range correlations, motivating geometric priors instead.

children.title: 3 Geometric Priors
children.gist: Two geometric priors—symmetry and scale separation—provide the inductive bias needed to learn in high dimensions, and combining local equivariant maps, coarsening and global invariance yields a general blueprint realised by existing architectures.
children.question: Geometric priors — what structural assumptions let neural networks beat the curse of dimensionality? (a blueprint of four building blocks)

children.title: Signals on a domain
children.gist: Machine learning systems act on signals defined over a domain with geometric structure, and the two routes to overcoming high dimensionality are exploiting symmetry and exploiting scale separation, as in convolutional filters and pooling.

children.title: 3.1 Symmetries, Representations, and Invariance
children.gist: Symmetries of a domain form a group whose representations act on signals, and functions built to be invariant or equivariant to these actions gain a powerful inductive bias, as shown by shift-invariant classification versus shift-equivariant segmentation.

children.title: 3.2 Isomorphisms and Automorphisms
children.gist: Different levels of structure on a domain, from bare sets to metric spaces, each have their own symmetry group, and distinguishing self-mappings from mappings between different objects clarifies what counts as a symmetry in each case.

children.title: 3.3 Deformation Stability
children.gist: Because real-world transformations are rarely exact symmetries, replacing strict invariance with a softer notion of stability to small deformations of the signal or domain lets models tolerate noise while remaining geometrically principled.

children.title: 3.4 Scale Separation
children.gist: Multiscale, spatially localised representations like wavelets are stable under small deformations where global Fourier representations are not, and hierarchically coarsening the domain lets functions separate long-range interactions into local ones.

children.title: 3.5 The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: Because purely linear invariant functions collapse signals to a trivial average, rich stable architectures must compose local equivariant layers, nonlinearities, coarsening, and a global invariant layer—the Geometric Deep Learning blueprint realised by CNNs and GNNs.
children.sourceHeading: 3.5 The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning

children.title: 4 Geometric Domains: the 5 Gs
children.gist: Five geometric domains—sets and graphs, grids, groups, manifolds with geodesics, and gauge fields on bundles—each carry their own symmetry structure, from which convolution-like operations can be systematically derived.
children.question: The 5 Gs — what distinct symmetry structures underlie grids, graphs, groups, geodesics and gauges? (five domain types)

children.title: 4.1 Graphs and Sets
children.gist: Graphs model systems of relations with a minimal permutation symmetry, and functions on them must be invariant or equivariant to node reordering, achieved by aggregating neighbourhood features with permutation-invariant functions such as sums.

children.title: 4.2 Grids and Euclidean spaces
children.gist: Grids are graphs with fixed node ordering whose natural symmetry is translation rather than permutation, and this symmetry alone forces linear shift-equivariant operators to be convolutions, with the Fourier transform as their shared eigenbasis.

children.title: 4.3 Groups and Homogeneous spaces
children.gist: Convolution and the Fourier transform generalise from Euclidean translations to any symmetry group acting on a homogeneous space, as shown by extending grid convolution to spherical convolution, though practical use is limited to small or low-dimensional groups.

children.title: 4.4 Geodesics and Manifolds
children.gist: Manifolds generally lack a global symmetry group, but their intrinsic distance structure still supports isometry-invariant convolutions built from geodesics, parallel transport, the exponential map and the Laplacian, though a consistent local frame is hard to define everywhere.

children.title: 4.5 Gauges and Bundles
children.gist: A gauge is a local choice of basis for the feature space attached to each point of a domain, and functions built on manifolds must be equivariant not just to domain symmetries but to arbitrary changes of this local frame, called gauge symmetry.

children.title: 4.6 Geometric graphs and Meshes
children.gist: Meshes sit between graphs and manifolds, letting discrete Laplacians, spectral filters, and functional maps between differently-discretised versions of the same surface support convolutions that are stable under remeshing and isometric deformation.

children.title: 5 Geometric Deep Learning Models
children.gist: Enforcing the Geometric Deep Learning blueprint on each domain recovers CNNs, group-equivariant CNNs, GNNs, Transformers, equivariant message passing, mesh CNNs, and gated RNNs as special cases of one scheme.
children.question: GDL models — how does one blueprint give rise to CNNs, GNNs, Transformers and RNNs alike? (eight architecture families)

children.title: Realising the blueprint
children.gist: Having established the Geometric Deep Learning blueprint across domains, the text now shows how enforcing it concretely yields the most popular deep learning architectures in current use.

children.title: 5.1 Convolutional Neural Networks
children.gist: Convolutional Neural Networks instantiate the translation-equivariant blueprint directly, combining local linear filters, nonlinearities, multiscale pooling, residual connections, and normalisation to enable very deep yet trainable models.

children.title: 5.2 Group-equivariant CNNs
children.gist: Generalising convolution from translations to larger discrete or continuous symmetry groups, such as 3D rotations or DNA's reverse-complement symmetry, yields group-equivariant CNNs implementable as filter-transform-then-convolve or spectral operations.

children.title: 5.3 Graph Neural Networks
children.gist: Graph Neural Networks realise permutation equivariance by aggregating neighbourhood features through one of three flavours—convolutional, attentional, or message-passing—that trade off expressiveness against computational cost.

children.title: 5.4 Deep Sets, Transformers, and Latent Graph Inference
children.gist: Treating a graph's edge set as empty, complete, or learned recovers Deep Sets, Transformers' self-attention, and latent graph inference respectively, showing these popular architectures as special cases of the GNN blueprint.
children.sourceHeading: 5.4 Deep Sets, Transformers, and Latent Graph Inference

children.title: 5.5 Equivariant Message Passing Networks
children.gist: For graphs whose node features include spatial coordinates, such as molecules, message-passing layers can be made equivariant to rigid Euclidean motions by depending only on inter-node distances, with richer representation-based approaches extending this further.

children.title: 5.6 Intrinsic Mesh CNNs
children.gist: Deep learning on meshes approximates manifold convolution by discretising geodesic patches around each node, and must handle the ambiguity of the local reference frame via isotropic filters, fixed gauges, angular pooling, or gauge-equivariant message passing.

children.title: 5.7 Recurrent Neural Networks
children.gist: Recurrent Neural Networks summarise sequential inputs step by step through a shared update function, and under suitable padding and fixed-point conditions this update exhibits a restricted form of translation equivariance across time steps.

children.title: 5.8 Long Short-Term Memory networks
children.gist: Gated RNNs like the LSTM use learned input, forget and output gates to combat vanishing gradients, and this gating mechanism is exactly the form required for invariance to time-warping, explaining their strength at modelling long-range dependencies.

children.title: 6 Problems and Applications
children.gist: Geometric Deep Learning already drives real-world systems across chemistry, biology, recommendation, traffic, vision, games, language, medicine, physics, and virtual reality.
children.question: Applications — where is Geometric Deep Learning already deployed at scale? (ten application domains)

children.title: Chemistry and Drug Design
children.gist: Graph neural networks accelerate costly drug discovery by virtually screening candidate molecules and by repositioning already-approved drugs for new purposes, exemplified by the discovery of the antibiotic Halicin and drug-interaction prediction.

children.title: Protein biology
children.gist: Representing proteins as contact graphs or molecular surface meshes lets graph and mesh neural networks predict protein function and design new binding proteins, as in DeepMind's AlphaFold and the MaSIF immunotherapy pipeline.

children.title: Recommender Systems and Social Networks
children.gist: Graph representation learning scaled to billions of edges now powers production recommender systems like Pinterest's PinSage and Amazon's P-Companion, as well as misinformation detection models that trace how news spreads through user networks.

children.title: Traffic forecasting
children.gist: Modelling road networks as graphs lets graph neural networks predict estimated time of arrival more accurately than prior methods, now deployed in production in Google Maps and Baidu Maps.

children.title: Object recognition
children.gist: Translation-equivariant convolutional networks drove the ImageNet-era breakthroughs in image classification and object detection, with architectures like AlexNet, VGG, and ResNet surpassing human-level accuracy.

children.title: Game playing
children.gist: Convolutional networks acting as translation-invariant feature extractors over grid-like game states enabled reinforcement learning milestones such as AlphaGo, AlphaZero, MuZero, and Agent57.

children.title: Text and speech synthesis
children.gist: One-dimensional grid architectures—dilated convolutions like WaveNet and self-attention-based Transformers like GPT and BERT—now dominate text and speech generation, translation, and language understanding.

children.title: Healthcare
children.gist: Grid-based CNNs, mesh networks for organ surfaces, graph networks for brain connectivity, and patient-similarity graphs are each being applied across diagnosis, prognosis and neurological disease prediction in medicine.

children.title: Particle physics and astrophysics
children.gist: Because particle collision and detector data naturally form unordered sets or graphs rather than grids, Geometric Deep Learning methods including equivariant and symmetry-aware networks are now used for jet classification and neutrino detection.

children.title: Virtual and Augmented Reality
children.gist: Mesh convolutional networks addressing deformable shape correspondence and synthesis underlie motion-capture pipelines for 3D body and hand avatars used in special effects and augmented reality products.

children.title: 7 Historic Perspective
children.gist: The role of symmetry in Geometric Deep Learning continues a millennia-long intellectual tradition running from ancient geometry through group theory and physics into early neural network design.
children.question: Historic perspective — how far back does the use of symmetry as an organising principle go? (a timeline from antiquity to CNNs)

children.title: Symmetry through the ages
children.gist: Symmetry has shaped human understanding of order and beauty since antiquity, from Pythagorean geometry and Platonic solids to Kepler's explanation of snowflakes through hexagonal packing.

children.title: Symmetry in Mathematics and Physics
children.gist: Group theory, developed by Galois, Lie, Klein and Cartan, became mathematics' language for symmetry, and Noether's theorem showed that every physical symmetry implies a conservation law, culminating in gauge theory's unification of fundamental forces.

children.title: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning
children.gist: Symmetry entered machine learning early through equivariant feature detectors and the limits proven by Minsky and Papert's Group Invariance Theorem, culminating in Fukushima's shift-invariant Neocognitron and LeCun's convolutional neural networks.
children.sourceHeading: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning
